sources.title: Call of Duty publisher apologizes for using real footage of Itaewon crowd crush | Yonhap News Agency
sources.text:
Call of Duty publisher apologizes for using real footage of Itaewon crowd crush | Yonhap News Agency Go to Contents Go to Navigation Facebook X More Pinterest Linked in Tumblr Reddit Facebook Messenger Copy URL URL is copied. OK SEOUL, Oct. 30 (Yonhap) -- The makers behind the Call of Duty video game apologized Friday for using real footage of the deadly 2022 Seoul crowd crush in its latest installment of the game and agreed to remove the footage. A short clip showing a paramedic performing CPR on a crowd crush victim lying on the street appeared in the opening moments of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4. The footage was used to depict a scenario of civilian casualties during a fictional war with North Korea. "We deeply apologize to the victims and their bereaved families who must have suffered, as well as to everyone who we have caused concern," Activision Publishing Inc. said in a notice to local reporters. "The footage will be removed in our update set to be rolled out on Nov. 12." The publisher added it had no plans to evoke tragic events, including the Itaewon crowd crush, when using news footage in its games, nor had it intended to ignore the pain caused by the accident. A total of 159 people were killed in a narrow alleyway in Seoul's night life district of Itaewon during Halloween festivities on Oct. 29, 2022. Bereaved families of the victims have criticized the game publisher for "lacking common sense" by using such footage and demanded a complete removal of the clip. sources.title: Korea ends Itaewon crush probe; prosecutors clear Mayor Oh and others - CHOSUNBIZ
sources.text:
Korea ends Itaewon crush probe; prosecutors clear Mayor Oh and others
The Joint Investigation Team of prosecutors and police for uncovering the truth about the deadly crowd crush in the nightlife district of Itaewon (hereafter the joint team) ended operations on the 30th. It came 14 months after it was launched in July last year on the orders of President Lee Jae-myung.
The Supreme Prosecutors' Office said in a media notice on the 30th that, "With the revised Criminal Procedure Act and other laws taking effect on Oct. 2, the joint team's operations will end that day." The revised Criminal Procedure Act centers on a full abolition of prosecutors' investigative authority.
The joint team said it conducted investigations at the request of the special investigation committee on the deadly crowd crush in the nightlife district of Itaewon, the bereaved families' council, and individual bereaved families, and issued non-indictment decisions the previous day on parts where it was difficult to recognize charges. Cases requiring continued investigation were transferred to the Korean National Police Agency.
The joint team was set up at the Seoul Western District Prosecutors' Office on July 30 last year, about two years and nine months after the deadly crowd crush in the nightlife district of Itaewon, following instructions from President Lee Jae-myung. It later indicted without detention former Yongsan Fire Station Chief Choi Seong-beom on Apr. 24 on charges of occupational negligence resulting in death and injury, following a request for investigation from the special investigation committee on the deadly crowd crush in the nightlife district of Itaewon, while issuing a non-indictment decision for former Yongsan Fire Station on-site command team leader Lee Bong-hak, who was referred for investigation together.
In the case involving numerous defamatory posts targeting victims and bereaved families, three people, including a judicial scrivener identified as A, were sent to trial in custody in January. A is accused of repeatedly posting writings and videos claiming, among other things, that the disaster occurred due to a "drug terror" attack.
By contrast, allegations of dereliction of duty by former acting National Fire Agency commissioner Nam Hwa-young, who was accused of neglecting duties as head of the Central Emergency Rescue Control Group at the time of the disaster, resulted in a non-indictment decision. Allegations that former Yongsan District Chief Park Hee-young destroyed evidence by replacing a mobile phone after the disaster also resulted in a non-indictment decision, with prosecutors saying the charges were difficult to substantiate.
Allegations of occupational negligence resulting in death and injury by Seoul Mayor Oh Se-hoon, who was accused of failing to take necessary measures before the disaster, and allegations of dereliction of duty by officials of the Ministry of the Interior and Safety, who were accused of leaving false report contents unaddressed during the disaster, also resulted in non-indictment decisions. The decisions came after reviewing closed-circuit (CC)TV footage, mobile phone forensic data, statements from related persons, and related legal principles.
The Supreme Prosecutors' Office said, "Even after the joint investigation team ends operations and after the transition to the public prosecution office, we will ensure there is no gap in investigations through substantive cooperation with the police."

Melbourne community theatre company catfished over ticket sales
Upstage Theatre Company co-founder Scott Hili says they fell victim to a catfish incident during their production of Jesus Christ Superstar. ( Supplied: Norrington Media )
The Upstage Theatre Company based in Melbourne's south-east says it was caught up in a catfishing scam.
A person claiming to be from a church asked them to set aside about 150 tickets for its recent production of Jesus Christ Superstar, before disappearing at the last minute.
Co-founder Scott Hili says it was a "kick in the teeth", with the theatre company now considering the prospect of closure.
A suburban theatre company was left with more than 150 empty seats and lost $7,500 in ticket sales after being catfished by someone claiming to represent a Melbourne church.
Scott Hili, co-founder of Upstage Theatre Company in Pakenham, in Melbourne's south-east, said the not-for-profit he and his husband began two years ago may have to eventually close if they can't fundraise the shortfall.
The situation began when Mr Hili received an enquiry for a large number of tickets to a recent matinee performance of Jesus Christ Superstar.
"We had about 220 people booked. And then I got an email inquiry for 157 tickets, which was the exact amount that was left," he said.
He googled the church, blocked off the seats and even opened up some more space.
"They were back and forth, they were very prompt with replying and they were able to give me all this information," Mr Hili said.
The local theatre group says it lost about $7,500 in promised ticket sales. ( Supplied: Norrington Media )
But as the date drew nearer and the invoice he had sent remained unpaid, Mr Hili prodded them for payment.
The person behind the email promised that a priest would take care of it. After two more attempts, and a phone call to the church, who knew nothing about it, Mr Hili realised they had been catfished.
While he quickly released the block on the seats, he said it was too late to sell any more tickets for that particular performance.
Mr Hili said the incident was a "kick in the teeth" for their theatre company.
"We're putting in our own money to provide the community with opportunities to do what they love, so we want to keep doing that," he said.
"Someone has intentionally sat there, created an email, created a persona and went to the trouble of actually booking tickets and committing to buying them, and then ghosting us.
He said cast members, who'd been initially expecting a full house, were also left disappointed.
"It's the intent, right? That's what hurts the most."
Mr Hili is now considering fundraising options to try to keep the theatre afloat and pay about $8,000 owed to various people for the production.
"In a financial crisis where the cost of living is high, we're already struggling as a new starting company."
A Victoria Police spokesperson confirmed they had received a report regarding a fraudulent ticket reservation, which was thoroughly assessed by local police.
"A review of the relevant legislation determined that because no property or financial advantage was obtained by the sender, the incident does not meet the strict legal threshold for a criminal deception offence," police said in a statement.
However, the spokesperson said police strongly encouraged community and non-profit organisations to review their booking and ticketing policies to protect themselves from similar incidents.
Mr Hili shared his theatre's experience with other local theatre companies in the hope of preventing the same thing happening elsewhere.
The Victorian Drama League, the state's peak body for community theatre, also distributed the warning to its members.
Challenges very real for many theatre companies
League president Susan Rundle

sources.title: Activision removes Seoul crush footage from Call of Duty after backlash - Mjengo Hub
sources.text:
Video clips showing the aftermath of a deadly crowd crush in Seoul will be removed from the latest Call of Duty video game after an angry reaction from victims' families.
Activision and developer Infinity Ward face criticism after real-life news coverage from a fatal crowd crush in Seoul appeared in Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4. The video clips, taken from the 2022 Itaewon district disaster in South Korea, were used in the game to illustrate a fictional invasion scenario.
The 10.29 Itaewon Disaster Bereaved Families Association expressed strong disapproval of the footage being included in an entertainment product, calling the choice senseless. Relatives of those who lost their lives in the tragedy, which claimed nearly 160 lives, stated that using actual footage of emergency personnel responding to the scene caused significant distress.
In a public statement, publisher Activision clarified that the opening cinematic utilises real-world news broadcasts to set up the fictional narrative of the title. The company stated that the inclusion was not intended to reference or trivialise the Itaewon disaster or any other real-world event. Activision extended condolences to the victims and confirmed that a game update scheduled for November 12 will permanently remove the clips from the game.
The association welcomed Activision's decision to remove the archived footage, but noted that the publisher had not contacted the group directly to issue a direct apology. The development team has previously faced scrutiny regarding how real-world historical conflicts and locations are referenced in video game campaigns.

Echidna sightings on Aboriginal-owned Lungatalanana/Clarke Island excite after extensive bushfires
New trail camera footage from Tasmania's Lungtalanana/Clarke Island raises hopes that the echidna population is recovering.
In 2014, a bushfire destroyed 98 per cent of the vegetation on the Aboriginal-owned island.
A restoration project hopes to return the island to its pre-colonial state.
Ranger Tasha Cooper had been learning how to trap feral cats on an island off Tasmania when she came across a discovery that sent her scrambling for her radio.
Curled up in the cage was an echidna — or trimanya in palawa kani , the language of Tasmania's Aboriginal people.
The species had not been encountered in person on the Bass Strait island in decades.
An echidna that wandered into a cage used to trap feral cats. ( Supplied: Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre )
Trail cameras have since recorded echidnas at four separate locations across the island. ( Supplied: Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre )
"Just to see this trimanya curled up trying to push his way out of this cage, there were just no words for it," she said.
'Australia's loneliest echidna' spotted on trail camera
An echidna dubbed "Australia's loneliest" by WWF after it was spotted on a trail camera on Lungtalanana in November 2023. ( Supplied: Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre )
Lungtalanana, also known as Clarke Island, is in the Furneaux group of islands off Tasmania's north-east coast.
About 8,230 hectares in size, the island returned to Aboriginal ownership in 2005.
Pakana rangers are working to restore the island through land management practices, including weed removal, cultural burning and remote wildlife monitoring.
In 2023, a trail camera recorded two images of an echidna, captured months apart.
Increased echidna sightings across the island have excited conservation crews. ( Supplied: Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre )
Due to the high number of images to review, the photos were not discovered until 2024.
It marked the first time the species had been spotted on Lungtalanana/Clarke Island in decades, and came after fears that a 2014 bushfire that burnt through 80 per cent of the island had wiped them out.
The rewilding program hopes to restore Lungatalanana/Clarke Island's vegetation, 98 per cent of which was destroyed in the 2014 bushfire. ( Supplied: WWF Australia/Chris Crerar )
Conservationist group WWF Australia, which supports the island's Aboriginal-led restoration project, had labelled the echidna as "Australia's loneliest".
Following the discovery, trail camera surveillance was boosted, with an image of an echidna recorded in 2025, and a further three this year.
But it was not until Ms Cooper's encounter in September that an echidna was spotted out in the field.
Pakana ranger Tasha Cooper was overcome with excitement when she discovered an echidna in a cat trap. ( Supplied: Tasha Cooper )
To determine whether the images were of a single active individual or multiple echidnas, rangers contacted University of Tasmania echidna expert Stewart Nicol.
Professor Nicol said that due to the "cryptic" nature of echidnas, it was difficult to estimate population numbers without tracking them.
"Given the size of the island that they're working on, and the fact that there's been about four or five sightings now, I'd be surprised if there were fewer than a dozen of them.
Associate Professor Stewart Nicol tracking echidnas on a separate project. ( 936 ABC Hobart: Carol Rääbus )

The discovery comes after the Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre last month launched the Lungtalanana Restoration Project.

sources.title: North Korea denies being behind $6.3bn Binance crypto hack - BBC News
sources.text:
Image source, Reuters Image caption, Kim Yo Jong, the sister of North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un By Osmond Chia Business reporter Published 3 November 2026
North Korea has denied claims that it was behind the record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance , calling the allegations "absurd rhetoric".
Kim Yo Jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un , said on Tuesday that the accusations are another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage Pyongyang's public image.
The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Secret Service and cyber analysts have said North Korea orchestrated the hack, which has been described as the largest in history.
This is the latest hack to be linked to North Korea, which has been accused of relying on cyber-crime to help finance its sanctioned economy.
Blockchain analysts and the FBI have said the attack was led by state-backed hacking group TraderTraitor.
The FBI has called on industry partners to help block transactions involving cryptocurrency accounts linked to the group.
"The US has made a trite provocation of linking it with the Democratic People's Republic of Korea again," Kim Yo-jong, the director of North Korea's General Affairs Department, said in a statement.
"It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads the international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds," she said.

Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far Published 5 days ago
But Pyongyang has been blamed for a number of major cyber attacks in recent years - accusations that it has denied.
The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record $1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025.
Pyongyang has systematically built its cyber operations, recruiting promising students from universities and sending them to hacker units overseen by North Korea's intelligence agency, research groups like the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies think tank have said.
The country has consistently denied such claims.
Kim Yo Jong said "it is the consistent policy stand of the DPRK government to resolutely oppose all sorts of malicious acts in cyberspace".

Who is Kim Yo-jong? Video, 00:02:32 Who is Kim Yo-jong? Published 16 June 2020
Binance did not respond to the BBC's queries about North Korea's alleged involvement in the hack.
Since the incident, the crypto giant has largely focused its public statements on the technical nature of the breach and its response to protect users.
The company's spokesperson said that a net $4.72bn has been withdrawn from the exchange since transactions resumed on Sunday.
The net outflow represents a "relatively limited portion" of Binance's total assets, which stand at approximately $157bn, the spokesperson told the BBC on Tuesday.
That figure reflects the impact of the hack, subsequent withdrawals and market price changes.
"Withdrawal levels are stabilising to what we would consider normal and expected on-chain activity," she added.
The company said last week that initial checks indicated that an engineer's laptop had been compromised, enabling an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals.
Trading in major cryptocurrencies on Binance has since resumed after the exchange worked with issuers to freeze assets impacted by the hack.
The company has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack and that it has so far covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach.

(EDITORIAL from The Korea Times on Nov. 5) | Yonhap News Agency Go to Contents Go to Navigation Facebook X More Pinterest Linked in Tumblr Reddit Facebook Messenger Copy URL URL is copied. OK Joint registration of taekwondo in order Seoul's misstep should be acknowledged; UNESCO should allow joint registration South Korea, which globally popularized the martial art form of taekwondo, is waking up to find North Korea has already moved to register the sport on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage List. A technical advisory body is soon expected to recommend registration of "Taekwon-Do, traditional martial art in the Democratic People's Republic of Korea" for North Korea's solo application, submitted in March 2024. The final decision will be made in Xiamen, China, at the meeting of the Intergovernmental Committee for the Safeguarding of Intangible Cultural Heritage, scheduled for Nov. 30 to Dec. 5. If finalized, Seoul may be left scrambling to register taekwondo on its own. It does not have to be that way. The martial art has shared roots that predate the division of the two Koreas. There is already a precedent for joint registration, with both North and South Korea successfully collaborating on the 2018 registration of "ssireum" — a traditional Korean form of wrestling — on the UNESCO list. With only about one month remaining before the meeting in Xiamen, South Korea should revive the dormant spirit of sports diplomacy and draw on the same energy that uplifted taekwondo globally through the establishment of "dojang" drill halls, as well as its adoption as an Olympic sport. It is regrettable that South Korea, a country so closely associated with taekwondo, has been left scrambling to secure its own UNESCO listing, having submitted its application only this year. Inscription on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage List does not give any country exclusive ownership of a cultural tradition. However, strained relations between the two Koreas have made a joint application more difficult. Regardless of the political climate, genuine efforts to preserve and uphold traditional culture must continue. Although South and North Korea both can claim taekwondo — the origins of which predate the division of the peninsula following the 1950-53 Korean War — the martial art has evolved along distinct paths in each country. The differences are reflected in two separate governing bodies: South Korea's World Taekwondo (WT) and the International Taekwondo Federation (ITF), which is associated with North Korea. South Korea helped popularize taekwondo internationally through WT's dojang system, which emphasizes Olympic-style competition and protective equipment. The ITF, meanwhile, places greater emphasis on traditional martial arts training, including direct contact. These groups have not always been at odds. In 2018, under the President Moon Jae-in administration, the leaders of both Koreas showed a spirit of cooperation, agreeing to work for the growth and integration of taekwondo in a meeting at Yanggakdo International Hotel in Pyongyang. The discussions at the time included the possibility of working for joint registration for UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list. Deteriorating inter-Korean relations, compounded by North Korea's constitutional amendment to define South Korea as a hostile state, have made cooperation increasingly difficult. Still, the legacy of assertive, state-led sports diplomacy has also been lacking. South Korea should consider whether it has grown too accustomed to the global success of its popular culture, taking its international influence for granted while overlooking the need to actively promote and preserve its traditional cultural heritage. The spirit of sports diplomacy that enabled South Korea to play a pivotal role in taekwondo's adoption as an Olympic event should not go to waste. Since North Korea joined Russia's war against Ukraine and began reaping economic benefits from the alliance, Pyongyang has become unresponsive to Seoul's overtures. Nevertheless, South Korea must draw on the legacy of its successful sports diplomacy and make every effort to define, promote and preserve its traditional cultural identity. UNESCO should take the circumstances surrounding the two Koreas and their shared martial arts heritage into account before recommending a separate inscription for North Korea. It should allow time for the two sides to pursue the possibility of a joint inscription. The times and the political context may be different than when the two Koreas worked together to obtain ssireum's Intangible Cultural Heritage inscription. In spirit, taekwondo remains the heritage of the people of both Koreas. UNESCO, as an organization committed to international cooperation in education, the sciences and culture, can provide an opportunity for the two Koreas to consult on the joint registration of taekwondo. Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Official figures show the economy has proved resilient in response to the jump in oil and gas prices. Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian Analysis Interest rate rise in midst of cost of living crisis will leave many incredulous Phillip Inman Bank’s decision goes contrary to analysis from Office for Budget Responsibility that predicts lower inflation and little impetus for wage growth Bank of England raises interest rates to 4%
An interest rate rise by the Bank of England to 4% is a big call when households are suffering from a second cost of living crisis in four years.
Many people will be incredulous when they hear of the decision to increase the cost of borrowing by 0.25 percentage points, looking around their neighbourhood for signs of a booming economy.
The official figures show the economy has proved resilient in response to the jump in oil and gas prices after the outbreak of war in Iran, but UK high streets are struggling and the underlying drivers of inflation are absent.
Most households are spending to stand still, whether it is on food, energy, holidays or leisure pursuits.
Businesses are in much the same position. Like households, they have absorbed significant tax rises.
What the Bank’s policymakers believe is that despite all this, the energy price shock, being larger than first estimated, will surge through all parts of the economy, forcing up prices, encouraging a wave of wage demands that will, in turn, give inflation a second burst of life next year and the following year.
This analysis stands in contrast to the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), which acts as the Treasury’s independent forecaster. The OBR was clear in evidence to parliament on Wednesday that there was little impetus for strong wages growth.
The OBR said that, rather than economic growth next year of 1.6% and a rise in inflation to 4.9%, as the Bank expects, it believes the economy will expand by just 1% in 2027 and that the consumer prices index (CPI) will peak at just 3.75%. Inflation hit 3.5% in September, official figures showed .
OBR chief economist, David Miles, said one of the main reasons for this assesment was the state of UK businesses, which he judged to be quite weak.
He said they had absorbed a large slice of the rise in energy and fuel costs, and their profit margins had plummeted on average as a result. Where once margins averaged 13% to 14%, the latest figures show they have fallen to 10% to 11%.
He said there would be little appetite to pay high wage settlements and the imperative would be to rebuild margins.
The wider economic situation is also very different from the previous crisis in 2022, when the country was coming out of the pandemic and dealing with the onset of the Ukraine war.
Back then, households were awash with lockdown savings that they wanted to spend, and firms were struggling to hire enough staff, leading to intense competition for workers and a spike in wages.
Today, savings are low and households bear the scars of four years of high inflation.
What sectors of the economy are making hay in 2026? Retailers and hospitality businesses are suffering, transport companies are battered by high costs and the charity sector is facing widespread financial difficulties.
Businesses in better performing sectors like banking and oil and gas also show little appetite for big wage increases. Vacancies are low, revealing that firms have no need to employ more people.
The Bank’s own survey of businesses and a separate report from its regional agents indicate “that wage and price expectations have moved little since September”.

Speaking on an earnings call with analysts on Thursday, Hua Hong chairman and president Bai Peng said the company planned to significantly expand its footprint in silicon photonics – a critical technology used in [AI optical modules](https://www.scmp.com/tech/tech-trends/article/3368817/globalfoundries-sees-strong-demand-chinese-optical-modules-amid-data-centre-boom?module=inline&pgtype=article) – during its next major capacity expansion in 2027.

“We want to participate in all silicon-based devices [inside optical modules],” Bai said, adding the sector is one of the two areas – along with power management chips – in which it wants to add “significantly more capacity”.

The plan underscores how the chip foundry is seeking to capture the next wave of the AI hardware boom, as rising wafer prices and shipments helped it achieve robust earnings for the third quarter.

For the three months ended September 30, the Shanghai-based chipmaker’s net profit surged 147 per cent year on year to US$123.4 million, according to its stock exchange filing on Thursday.

Total revenue hit a record US$987.1 million, a nearly 20 per cent year-on-year increase. That was partly driven by the integration of its newly acquired subsidiary Huali Microelectronics, aimed at bolstering the company’s advanced manufacturing capacity.

Excluding the figures from Huali Microelectronics, the firm’s total revenue reached US$803.4 million, beating the company’s previous guidance of US$770 million to US$780 million.

The AI boom had “caught most people by surprise”, Bai said. He likened the current AI infrastructure buildout to the early days of the internet, calling semiconductor chips “the new oil of the industrial age”.

sources.title: Spain's rail authorities face European fraud probe after Urda rail disaster - BBC News
sources.text:
Image source, EPA Image caption, Last month's train crash in which 69 people died was the second deadly accident on the same high-speed line this year By Alba Morgade Published 5 hours ago
European Union prosecutors have begun investigating the possible misuse of EU funds meant for upgrading the Spanish railway line where a train crash killed 69 people last week.
Prosecutors backed by a special unit of Spain's Guardia Civil security force said they were conducting the inquiry at the offices of Adif rail infrastructure authority and rail safety agency AESF.
The 28 October accident on the Madrid-Seville high-speed line was one of the worst railway disasters in Europe this century.
It is the second EU fraud inquiry opened into Spain's railways this year, after 46 people were killed on the same line at Adamuz in January.
Last week, a train operated by state-owned operator Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to private Spanish company Iryo outside the village of Urda, around 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid.
The LZB communication system that monitors the position of trains had gone down, and the Renfe train had been given the all clear to start running at normal speed, even though the Iryo train ahead of it had been unable to restart.
The two accidents nine months apart on the same line have claimed 115 lives and dozens more injuries.
Shock of rail tragedy gives way to sorrow and outrage in politically divided Spain Published 29 October
Spanish transport minister resigns days after deadly train crash Published 3 days ago
The European Public Prosecutor's Office (EPPO) said on Friday it had begun conducting investigative measures at Spain's rail authorities "after the opening of an investigation into possible fraud affecting EU funds , external allocated to the renovation and upgrading of safety, signalling and communications systems on the Madrid-Seville high-speed railway line".
The EPPO highlighted high public interest in the case, but said no further details would be made public.
As part of the process, a Spanish judge assigned to the case has to ensure the investigation complies with legal safeguards, including authorising any measures that might involve house searches or phone-tapping.
Image source, EPA Image caption, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez (C) faces parliamentary elections on 29 November
The Urda disaster has damaged the Socialist-led government of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez ahead of a 29 November general election and the party is trailing the conservative People's Party (PP) in most opinion polls.
Close Sánchez ally Óscar Puente resigned this week as transport minister, after seeing two deadly accidents on his watch this year.
The PP and far-right Vox say Puente's resignation is not enough and they have demanded that Sánchez resign too.
Many people in Spain have now become wary of taking the train, with reports of widespread cancellations and empty station platforms.
A funeral for the 69 victims at Urda will take place on Tuesday at Toledo cathedral, in the same province that the disaster happened.
Puente's successor, Carlos Cuerpo, has vowed to take all necessary measures to "restore the confidence of Spaniards in our high-speed rail".
Cuerpo met survivors of January's Adamuz disaster on Friday and they handed him a list of 11 demands for improving safety on Spain's railways.

New Zealand election too close to call with 95% votes in Skip to content
Incumbent Luxon said his National Party has a 'pathway' to forming a government Image: David Rowland/REUTERS Advertisement The two main parties were effectively deadlocked in New Zealand 's close-fought general elections on Saturday, with the rising cost of living and general economic problems the main issues at stake.
Results with 95% votes counted showed the ruling center-right National Party and the opposition Labour Party neck-and-neck with just under 30% of the vote.
The National Party held a slim lead of about 3,500 votes more than Labour late on Saturday night.
PM claims 'pathway' to power as opposition calls for 'common ground'
Incumbent Prime Minister Cristopher Luxon, who heads the National Party, said that his party "is once again the largest party in parliament, and we have a pathway to forming the next government."
The National Party currently governs in coalition with the pro-business ACT and the right-wing populist New Zealand First. According to preliminary results, the three parties are set to net a total 67 seats in parliament, amounting to a wafer-thin majority.
Labour leader Chris Hipkins said that New Zealand's politicians would need to find "common ground" after the results showed neither his party nor the ruling National Party were likely to form a governing majority on their own.
"New Zealand has spoken. It may take us a little bit longer to figure out exactly what it is that you've said," Hipkins told supporters.
"Our next parliament is going to require all of us to compromise, to work together, and to find common ground."
What to know about the election results in New Zealand
Special votes, including those cast from people overseas, are to be counted over the next three weeks. The votes typically benefit left-leaning parties and have shifted preliminary election results over the last three elections.
Final results are expected to be released on November 27.
If the right-wing bloc fails to hold on to its slim majority, the centrist Opportunity Party could act as a kingmaker. The party is projected to get seven seats, putting it past the 5% threshold to enter parliament for the first time since it was founded in 2017.
Luxon has previously ruled out cooperating with the Opportunity Party.
New Zealand has a mixed-member proportional system that requires voters to tick two options: a party and a local electoral candidate.
Electorate winners earn a seat in parliament, which typically has 120 seats, unless a so-called "overhang" leads to more lawmakers being returned to parliament, along with the highest-ranked members of the party based on their national party vote.
Preliminary results on Saturday showed that parliament is set to expand to 130 seats because of the overhang, making it the largest parliament in New Zealand history.
The vote took against a backdrop of high prices for basic goods and the highest unemployment in more than a decade.
The voting took place under New Zealand's strict laws banning media reporting and political campaigning on the final day.
New Zealanders have, however, been able to cast their votes since October 26, with almost 1.7 million of the country's 3.8 million eligible voters already casting their ballots by Thursday, according to the electoral commission.

The Ministry of Interior and Safety said Wednesday it will launch a dedicated website for victims and bereaved families of the Oct. 29 Itaewon crowd crush on Thursday.
The site consolidates information on victim support and memorial projects in one place and provides a communication channel for bereaved families and survivors. Funded following a request from bereaved families last year, it has been under construction since May and goes live to mark the fourth anniversary of the tragedy. Support and memorial information had previously been available through the ministry's main website.
Visitors can check eligibility for support programs, application procedures and required documents, as well as updates on memorial projects and upcoming event schedules.
The site also introduces new features to help users get answers and connect with one another. Bereaved families and survivors can submit inquiries about support programs or memorial projects and receive personalized responses directly from the officials in charge. Users are notified when a response is posted so they can check the outcome.
The site also provides a shared space where bereaved families and survivors can exchange views, as well as separate dedicated spaces for each group to share information and stay in contact.
To ensure foreign bereaved families and survivors can easily access information on support and memorial programs, the site offers services in five languages: English, Chinese, Japanese, Russian and Persian.
Shin Ki-dong, head of the Oct. 29 Itaewon Crowd Crush Victim Relief and Memorial Support team, said he hopes the site will help bereaved families and survivors "more easily find answers to their questions, communicate with one another, and take small steps toward healing from the pain of the tragedy and returning to everyday life."

sources.title: Activision to Pull Real Seoul Tragedy Footage From 'Call of Duty' After Families Demand Removal
sources.text:
Activision to Pull Real Seoul Tragedy Footage From 'Call of Duty' After Families Demand Removal Visitors walks past a Call Of Duty Modern Warfare 4 placard during the preview night of Paris Games Week 2026 in Paris, on October 21, 2026. Photo by Simon WOHLFAHRT / AFP via Getty Images The Briefing Activision confirmed it will remove real footage from the 2022 Itaewon crowd crush — which killed 160 people in Seoul — from Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 via a game update on November 12.
The 10.29 Itaewon Disaster Bereaved Families Association and the Korea Game Users Association condemned the footage as "highly inappropriate and senseless," pressing Activision into a public apology.
The backlash erupted days before the fourth anniversary of the disaster, exposing what critics call a systemic failure in editorial oversight at one of gaming's largest publishers.
Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 , developed by Infinity Ward and published by Activision , centers on a fictional North Korean military invasion of South Korea. Released worldwide on October 23, 2026, the title blends invented news dispatches with archival broadcast material to manufacture a sense of documentary realism — a creative decision that quickly became a public crisis.
South Korean players were among the first to flag what appeared to be genuine footage from the 2022 Itaewon crowd crush, embedded within a cinematic sequence at the close of the game's first mission . The clip — approximately three seconds long — shows emergency workers performing CPR, victims lying in rows, and people transported on stretchers. For South Korean audiences who lived through that night, the images required no caption.
The Itaewon crowd crush unfolded during Halloween celebrations, when an enormous crowd compressed into a narrow alley in Seoul's Itaewon district and the pressure became unsurvivable. The surge killed 160 people and injured 196 — a death toll that continued to rise over subsequent years as trauma victims were officially recognized. Most of the dead were in their twenties.
October 29, 2026 marks the fourth anniversary of the disaster. The timing of the backlash — surfacing only days before that date — gave the controversy a gravity that Activision could not absorb quietly.
The 10.29 Itaewon Disaster Bereaved Families Association issued a statement — carried by SBS — describing the footage as deeply painful to witness. The group noted that rescuers and bystanders still carry psychological wounds from that night, and that placing those images inside an entertainment product designed for mass-market profit was, in their own words, "highly inappropriate and senseless." The families called on Activision to act without delay.
The Korea Game Users Association reinforced the demand, calling for the clip's removal, a clear explanation of how it entered the game's production pipeline, and a formal corporate apology.
Activision Apologizes and Sets a Removal Date
On October 28, Activision issued an initial statement acknowledging the use of real news footage but stopping short of committing to its removal. By October 30, under mounting pressure, the company distributed a fuller apology to South Korean media. Activision stated that the footage was included to create a "realistic and immersive experience" and insisted it had no intention of invoking or trivializing the Itaewon disaster. The company confirmed the footage would be fully excised through a game update on November 12.
The bereaved families' association acknowledged the decision but told the BBC that Activision had not reached out to them directly. No personal apology had been delivered to the families of the 160 victims.
The Industry Blind Spot Behind the Controversy
The episode reopens a long-standing debate about how studios mine the visual vocabulary of real disasters — fires, explosions, mass casualties — to give fictional conflict the weight of truth. The Modern Warfare franchise has tested those limits before, but this case is different in a specific way: the Itaewon footage did not evoke a distant or historical event. It captured a tragedy that South Korean players, their families, and emergency responders recognize from firsthand experience.
Commentators across the industry have pointed out that standard geographic and cultural review — the kind routinely applied to localized game releases — should have identified the clip before launch, especially given that Modern Warfare 4 centers its entire narrative on the Korean peninsula. The failure was not one of intent but of process: the assumption, still apparently widespread in major productions, that real suffering can serve as atmosphere at no cost to the people it represents.

sources.text:
Image source, Activision Image caption, Modern Warfare 4 locates players in a war between North and South Korea By Riyah Collins BBC Newsbeat Published 29 October 2026
Families who lost loved ones in a crush caused by overcrowding in Seoul's narrow streets four years ago say they're appalled to see footage of it on the latest Call of Duty game.
In an opening scene of Modern Warfare 4, video of rescue efforts from the 2022 disaster in Itaewon, South Korea, is used to show the aftermath of an imagined attack from North Korea.
Almost 160 people died and their families are calling on the game's makers Activision to delete the footage, saying including it was "senseless".
Activision confirmed it used recordings from that night but had "not intended to reference or trivialise the Itaewon disaster or any other real-world tragedy in any way, shape or form".
"In developing Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, we approached the subject matter with care and respect," a spokesperson said.
"The game's opening cinematic utilises some real world news coverage to establish the game's fictional narrative."
Thursday marks the fourth anniversary of the crush, which happened when more than 100,000 people went out in Seoul's nightlife district to celebrate Halloween.
The narrow streets became so tightly packed that people could not move and some were unable to breathe.
"We cannot help but be appalled that the chaotic and desperate scene, in which many citizens at the site performed CPR to save one another and victims lay on the freezing street, was used as it was to create a scene in a game," the bereaved families said.
"Using such an event as material for a game made for entertainment is in itself highly inappropriate and senseless," their statement continued.
"If the game developer has even a minimum of courtesy and empathy towards the victims, it should take corrective action without delay."
Activision did not comment on the request to edit the scene to remove the video from that night.
Modern Warfare 4, which was released last week, had already faced criticism for basing the game on North Korea invading South Korea, as the two countries have been technically at war for decades.
Fighting stopped in the Korean War in 1953, but the two countries never signed a peace treaty and conflict is a very real worry in that part of the world.
At the launch of the game, Call of Duty's chief marketing officer, Tyler Bahl, told Newsbeat: "We have to understand this is entertainment".

Facebook Twitter Print Email ‘Make or bake time’: Guterres urges climate justice pact as leaders gather at COP31 Conference coverage By Laura Quinones in Antalya 11 November 2026 Climate and Environment UN chief António Guterres called for a new global climate justice agreement at COP31 on Wednesday, urging governments to tax fossil fuel companies to help countries bearing the brunt of a crisis they did little to cause. His appeal came as world leaders gathered in Antalya amid unresolved questions over climate finance and the future of fossil fuels. Today at COP31 Leaders’ Summit: Guterres calls for climate justice and taxes on oil giants.

Today saw packed corridors at the COP31 conference venue in Antalya as world leaders arrived for a two-day high-level Summit, bringing tighter security, road closures and an early start for delegates, some of whom reached the venue as early as 5 a.m.
Those who arrived before dawn were rewarded with a spectacular sunrise. Later, at the opening ceremony, traditional Turkish dancing, colourful performances, videos and even a COP31 theme song gave the opening ceremony an unusually festive air for a gathering confronting one of the world’s most pressing crises.
But the day’s most memorable message came from the Secretary-General, who accused polluters of delaying action, and once again warned that the climate crisis is advancing faster than global efforts to contain it.
“Our planet is heating up. The clock is winding down. It’s make or bake time ,” he said, reminding world leaders that even if current national plans are fully implemented, the planet is heading towards more than 2.5°C of warming by century’s end.
But he insisted that breaching the 1.5°C threshold does not mean giving up. “Science is not telling us to surrender. It is telling us to fight harder” the UN chief said, stressing that every fraction of a degree of warming avoided matters.
Against that backdrop, the Secretary-General proposed a ‘climate justice compact’ to help developing countries move away from fossil fuels while protecting those already suffering from climate change.
“We cannot demand that countries transform their economies while denying them the means to do so,” he said.
The proposed compact rests on four priorities:
Accelerate the transition away from fossil fuels through national plans that protect workers and communities, while expanding renewable energy.
Protect vulnerable populations with early-warning systems, stronger adaptation measures and faster support after climate disasters.
Deliver affordable climate finance , with wealthy countries fulfilling their commitments and more investment reaching developing nations.
Strengthen international cooperation to overcome trade barriers, technological divides and geopolitical rivalries.
The UN chief took aim at fossil fuel interests, accusing them of distorting science and delaying climate action.
“Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs,” he declared. “The dinosaurs did not have a lobby. Fossil fuels do.”
He contrasted the $95 billion earned by the world’s nine largest oil companies in one quarter with the roughly $600 million received by the international fund helping vulnerable countries recover from climate-related loss and damage .
That was equivalent to just 14 hours of those companies’ profits, he said, urging governments to tax windfall profits.

sources.title: 'Call of Duty' uses Itaewon crowd crush footage, drawing outrage from victims' families - The Herald Business
sources.text:
SOCIETY 'Call of Duty' uses Itaewon crowd crush footage, drawing outrage from victims' families by Han Ji-suk Published : Oct. 29, 2026 - 12:55:24 View Korean Original
Game includes footage of bystanders performing CPR at the scene
Korea Game Users Association calls for explanation and apology
A first-person shooter game depicting a full-scale North Korean invasion of South Korea has drawn widespread backlash after footage from the Oct. 29 Itaewon crowd crush was found embedded in its opening sequence. Victims' families, civic groups and a gaming industry association condemned the move as "unconscionable" and called on the developer to remove the footage.
According to the gaming industry, "Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4," released by US game publisher Activision on Friday, includes roughly three seconds of broadcast archival footage showing bystanders performing CPR on a collapsed victim in the immediate aftermath of the Itaewon crowd crush.
The footage was used to depict civilian casualties in the game, which is set against the backdrop of a war on the Korean Peninsula.
The Oct. 29 Itaewon Crowd Crush Bereaved Families Association and the Citizens' Response Committee issued a joint statement Wednesday saying they "cannot help but be appalled" that footage of the chaotic and desperate scene — in which countless bystanders performed CPR on one another and victims lay on cold streets — was lifted wholesale to recreate a scene in a video game.
"Citizens who participated in rescue efforts or witnessed the disaster are still suffering from trauma," the groups said, calling the use of such an event for entertainment purposes "highly inappropriate and unconscionable." They also expressed concern that the game's setting was fueling secondary harm, with hateful comments online denigrating the disaster by linking it to the game's fictional scenario.
Jo In-young, co-director of the Citizens' Response Committee's joint situation room, told Yonhap that the incident reflected a profound insensitivity to the anguish felt by victims' families, survivors and the public when confronted with footage from the scene, and a failure to consider the dignity of those who died.
Jo added that foreign bereaved families had traveled to Korea to attend a memorial service, and that the committee planned to formally raise the issue with signatures from victims' families.
The Korea Game Users Association also issued a statement Wednesday urging Activision to provide "a clear explanation of the circumstances and an apology" for using footage of a tragic disaster unrelated to the game's narrative in a way that caused harm to victims' families and others. The association called on the company to "respond responsibly," including by releasing an update that replaces the footage.
Activision said it "had absolutely no intention of referencing or trivializing any real-world tragedy, including the Itaewon disaster."

sources.title: EU will examine Israel association agreement after massive public petition – POLITICO
sources.text:
The European Commission will examine its association agreement with Israel after more than 1.1 million EU citizens signed a petition asking it to do so.
"The Commission will meet the organisers [of the petition] to discuss the initiative in detail in the coming weeks. A public hearing will then be organised by the European Parliament," the EU executive said in a press release Thursday.
While the examination is unlikely to lead to any substantial changes to the status quo, the number of signatures shows the prominence of the issue of EU-Israel relations among the EU public — and will force the Commission to give an official response.
Out of 136 registered petitions — known as the EU Citizens' Initiative — in more than a decade, only 14 had reached the 1 million-signature threshold required to be officially brought in front of the EU executive.
The ECI mechanism requires the Commission to examine petitions signed by more than 1 million EU citizens from more than seven countries. Earlier this year, the Commission rejected a petition to expand abortion financing after it was signed by 1.2 million citizens.
The European Left Alliance, an umbrella group for 11 left-wing political parties, started the petition almost two years ago. The group said the EU should suspend its trade and political dialogue with Israel over what it sees as the country's failure to prevent genocide in Gaza.
France accounted for the most signatures with 339,479, followed by Italy with 283,863 and Spain with 151,821. The Commission will reply by May 2027 to say whether it plans to take any action in response to the petition.
Originally signed in 1995 and coming into force in 2000, the association agreement covers political dialogue and trade between the EU and Israel. The bloc is Israel’s biggest trading partner, accounting for about a third of its total trade in goods with the world in 2025, according to EU data .
The wars in Gaza and Lebanon have provoked vehement criticism of Israel and divided European leaders.

sources.text:
Image source, FBI Image caption, FBI redacted examples of the 900 victim videos secretly recorded by North Korean hackers By Kelly Ng Published 13 November 2026, 02:48 GMT
State-sponsored hackers from North Korea have taken more than $400 million in cryptocurrency by using fake video calls to steal people's identities, US authorities say.
More than 900 victims have fallen prey to the scheme, which the FBI refers to as FaceStealer, in the last 18 months, according to the bureau.
"The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years," says FBI cyber director Brett Leatherman.
This comes a week after the world's largest crypto exchange Binance revealed that hackers had used fake job interviews to steal a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) from the company.
US law enforcement agencies attributed the Binance hack, thought to be the largest crypto hack to date, to North Korea-linked actors. Pyongyang has denied this claim.
Authorities say FaceStealer, the latest scheme, "aggressively targets" those who work in the cryptocurrency and web3 sectors, particularly those who are involved in the development and maintenance of open-source software.
According to the FBI and US Justice Department, FaceStealer hackers use fake or hijacked social media accounts to invite potential victims into video calls hosted over "imposter versions" of Zoom, Microsoft Teams, and Google Meet.
Next, the hackers play pre-recorded videos of previous victims the target is acquainted with to simulate a legitimate call – except that the audio would appear to malfunction.
A message then pops up on the target's screen, asking them to "fix" the audio by clicking on a link. This "fix" would eventually download malware onto the target's device, which allows hackers to access their contact lists and apps, widening their pool of potential victims.
Hackers would secretly record these calls and use the recordings as material to scam their new victims, according to the US authorities.
The FBI has described FaceStealer as "a highly effective social engineering scheme capable of deceiving even the most experienced technical and security conscious computer user".
"It exploits our trust in ubiquitous video conference platforms and valued personal relationships," Patrick Grandy, assistant director in charge of the bureau's Los Angeles field office, said in a statement on Thursday.
"If you can't imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough."

‘Call of Duty’ publisher apologizes, says will remove Itaewon crowd crush footage Published : Oct. 30, 2026 - 15:18:35 Add The Korea Herald on Google
US publisher Activision has formally apologized for using footage from the 2022 Itaewon crowd crush in its latest “Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4” and said it will remove the footage entirely, according to MBC on Friday.
In a statement sent to the Korean TV channel, Activision said the problematic footage would be completely removed through a game update scheduled for release on Nov. 12.
“We offer our deepest condolences and sincere apologies to the bereaved families, victims and everyone who has been deeply hurt or distressed by this incident,” the company said in a statement.
Activision reiterated that the game is a work of fiction designed to deliver a realistic, immersive experience. It said the use of actual news footage in the game was not intended to evoke any tragic event, including the Itaewon disaster, or to downplay the suffering it caused.
The move follows an outcry from families of the 159 victims of the Itaewon crowd crush, which occurred on Oct. 29, 2022, after footage from the disaster was found in the latest “Call of Duty” installment, which depicts a fictional all-out war on the Korean Peninsula.
The bereaved families and civic groups expressed dismay and called for the footage to be removed.

Modern Warfare 4 faces backlash after real footage of South Korean crowd crush tragedy was discovered in game's opening moments | Eurogamer.net
sources.text:
Activision has come under fire due to the inclusion of real-world footage of the tragic Itaewon Disaster in Modern Warfare 4. The bereaved families association and the Citizens Countermeasure Meeting are asking for the footage to be removed.
In its opening moments, short clips are used to represent a news report of fictional civilian casualties during a North Korean invasion of South Korea. These include archived news clips of a person being carried away on a stretcher, someone performing CPR on a victim, and multiple bodies laying on a road.
"Using such an incident as material for a game intended for entertainment purposes is itself highly inappropriate and a senseless act," the groups said in a joint statement ( thanks SBS news ).
"The Itaewon tragedy was a tragic disaster that produced hundreds of casualties, and citizens who participated in the rescue efforts or witnessed the event at the time continue to suffer from trauma. If the game developer has even a minimum level of courtesy and empathy toward the victims, they should promptly take corrective measures."
This statement was joined by another by The Korean Game Consumers Association, who wrote: "There must be a clear explanation of the circumstances and an apology regarding the fact that footage of a tragic disaster unrelated to the context of gameplay was utilized, causing harm to the bereaved families and others." It called for the footage to be replaced in an update, while also emphasising the controversy should not grow into a demand for censorship of the game.
Eurogamer contacted Activision for comment, and was provided the following statement: "In developing Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, we approached the subject matter with care and respect. The game’s opening cinematic utilizes some real world news coverage to establish the game’s fictional narrative. It is not intended to reference or trivialize the Itaewon disaster or any other real-world tragedy in any way, shape or form."
Today is the four year anniversary of the Itaewon crowd crush tragedy, in which 160 people died and a further 196 were injured. It is South Korea's most severe mass casualty event since the Sampoong Department Store collapse in 1995.
